CHAPTER IV 

Filing 

Good words shall gain you honor in the market place, but good deeds shall gain you friends among men.-Chinese proverb.

Importance of filing. The person who can file a letter and find it when it is wanted has one of the indispensable qualifications of a good secretary.

If you cannot produce a paper promptly when it is requested, you lose your employer's confidence; good will, which may have been created by painstaking work in other directions, is sacrificed through a single misstep in filing.

Regardless of how extensive or how elementary your filing system may be, you must have two basic qualifications—accuracy and a general knowledge of the principles of filing. Remember that the adjective accurate is not one which can be compared. 

You cannot be accurate, more accurate, most accurate; you are either accurate or inaccurate. 

Developing accuracy. Since filing cannot be checked like bookkeeping or typewriting, you will have to do it more carefully than any other part of your office work. There is a common tendency to look at a file, determine the approximate position of a folder, and then gaze in another direction when 88

Filing inserting the letter. That momentary carelessness often makes it necessary to look in surrounding files if a letter cannot be found in its proper place. However, these errors are really not so serious as those caused by a cursory glance at the name or filing title. A firm may be listed in your files as W. E. 

Kelly & Company. Your employer, who knows

Mr. Kelly, may unconsciously dictate one letter to 

Wade Kelly & Company. If you are not watchful in filing, this may be filed under W, a new folder being opened up for Wade, Kelly & Co. You will never know you have made a mistake until the letter is called for. A complete search of the files from 

K to W will be impossible, so the letter will be given up for lost until some day you find the "Wade" folder in going through the W section of the file. 

This type of error is even more common when no special folder must be made for the letter, but when the copy can be put in a general correspondence folder.

Filing is one of the secretarial duties for which you can sit down and calmly plan the best method of operation. (Of course, sitting down to work out the problem refers only to the original filing of a paper and not to locating one which has already been filed.) Never file anything until you are so well acquainted with its classification that you can find it again without hesitancy. If a file is already in operation, go through it and note the disposition that has been made of similar papers. Just because you are in a hurry to get rid of a certain letter is no

reason for misfiling it. It is wise to keep in mind that time spent in filing is gained in finding, a period when every second counts for more than does the same time when used in leisurely filing. 

Principles of filing.-To get the most out of your filing system, it is absolutely necessary that you understand the underlying principles upon which the various filing systems are built. Rarely is a single type used alone; rather, most files are built up on the combination of a number of principles. 

Summed up in three words, efficient operation in this part of your work is really filing and finding. 

One without the other is useless. While it is important that you learn filing principles for the sake of correctly placing papers, it is more important that you apply these principles so as to find a document when desired. Some inefficient people can expound the principles well, but are so careless in their application that their knowledge is useless. 

Never get the idea that filing is extremely difficult; really the principles underlying filing are easy to understand if they are studied in their simple form and with a constant view to their utilitarian purposes. Nevertheless, the necessity for constant vigilance in following a filing system does make its operation an ever-present burden.

Chronological filing. The simplest form of all filing systems is based on time sequence. A purely chronological file is often used for personal correspondence and bills. Each letter is put in the folder as it arrives, those coming the first of the

Filing month being placed at the bottom with those of each succeeding day on top. When the month is ended, the folder may either be destroyed or put away to be referred to if occasion arises. This type of file has an advantage in calling attention to correspondents who have been neglected for a long time.

Filing in chronological form is very simple; finding is more difficult. If you do not remember the exact day on which a letter came, you will be compelled to search through any number of letters received about that time until this particular one turns up. For this reason, the system must be supplemented by some other if the material handled becomes bulky. However, the chronological principle is carried through as a part of almost all other filing systems.

Alphabetical filing.-By far the most widely used form of filing is that built up on some alphabetical division of the material to be filed. The simplest form is that in which the names of the correspondents are arranged in alphabetical order. The letters received and sent to people whose names begin with A are placed just behind a guide marked A, and further classifications and guides are provided for the other letters of the alphabet. Certain little-used letters such as X, Y, and Z may be combined under one guide. If a straight alphabetical file becomes burdensome, subdivisions can be made by adding second, third, and even fourth letters to the respective initial guides. For example, one

guide may be BRAA, the following, BRAG, and the third, BRAN. Correspondence with a person named 

BRACE would be placed before the first guide; 

BRAMLEY before the second; and BRANDON before the third. Scientifically worked out subdivisions of the alphabet can be procured from any stationer. 

These printed tabs are usually much more satisfactory than trying to make a division of your own.

Difficulty in alphabetizing.-Alphabetic filing appears very easy on the surface, but give the average secretary two hundred letters to file under one letter of the alphabet and the results will be astonishing. An experiment with fifty-four students in a large high school revealed that only one student could arrange the letters correctly. Files were returned to some individuals as many as fourteen times before they could locate their errors. 

If this was true of high-school students, one can only guess at the condition of the files in offices where employees are not subject to systematic checking, and where many who use the files have not had the advantage of a good filing course. 

Under those conditions one should not be surprised that things cannot be located readily; perhaps it is even a miracle that they can be found at all. 

Spend enough time on alphabetizing to be able to recognize instantly a name that is out of order.

The degree to which this ability can be attained was illustrated recently by a little incident aboard a transatlantic liner. Shortly after leaving port,

Filing 

each person was given a passenger list. An hour later a wireless message was received for a man named Zucker. When consulted, the conductor of the tour said, "We have no one by that name. 

His secretary, who had reported for work only an hour before sailing, quickly brought the name on the passenger list to the attention of the conductor. 

When the message was dispatched to Mr. Zucker's stateroom, the conductor turned to his secretary and said, "That's odd; I thought I had familiarized myself with our passenger list. Do you know that fellow?" To this the girl replied, "No, I do not know him, but in glancing through the names of the passengers, I noticed that Zupke appeared before Zucker. As these were the only names not in proper sequence, they stood out from the rest." Would you, as a secretary, have detected such an error?

Rules for alphabetizing. If you are in doubt as to the placing of a name, it is best to consult the telephone directory. The compilers of these directories have spent a great deal of time in perfecting an alphabetic list which you can safely follow as an authority. However, you will be able to improve your own filing ability if you observe the following guides for alphabetic filing: 

1. The first letter is not enough to use in filing.

Subject filing.—In a great many instances you will find that the subject of certain correspondence is more important than the name of the correspondent. In such cases a subject file can be used to advantage. Subjects instead of names generally interspersed with a straight alphabetic file. In fact, the user of a file seldom stops to think whether he is filing by subject or by name. However, a mixture of both systems leaves the way open to many mistakes. The head of the secretarial department in a large college says that she cannot get girls to file under subject. If she directs a memorandum to E. H. Blake, head of the 

Psychology Department, the secretary will open up a new folder for Blake, E. H. instead of filing the memorandum under Psychology Department. 

Since lack of acquaintance with the file will cause such errors, it is well to take off a list of the filing titles in a medium-sized system and try to memorize these subjects. This feat is impossible, in working with a large file, but even a hasty glance through the file will tend to fix many of the subjects in your mind.

Filing Knowledge of business essential.-A strict subject file is less common in use, but no less important to understand. You cannot construct a subject file unless you are thoroughly familiar with the subject and all subdivisions of the material which is to be filed. For example, a young woman working for a dress manufacturer who is collecting all the information he can gather on the subject of women's garments would probably have little difficulty in handling a subject file in her work. She would not file a magazine article on slipper buckles under HATS. On the other hand, it takes an experienced person to manipulate a legal or library subject file. Professor Ripley, of Harvard, is the author of a book entitled, Trusts, Pools, and Combinations. 

The word trust here denotes combinations prohibited by the Federal anti-trust laws. A professor looked for this book in a library but could not find it on the proper shelf. It then occurred to him that if the librarian were ignorant of the subject, the book might have been placed among those on trust companies and banks. That is where he found Professor Ripley's book. Similar misplacements can be found in the work of many secretaries who are not familiar with the business for which they are keeping a file. 

Changing the subject base. Great care will have to be taken in shifting the base in the compilation of a subject file, for only by careful and intelligent handling will you secure logical headings and prevent duplication and confusion of subjects.

A subject should be sufficiently inclusive to embrace all material desired, but it should be equally exclusive, in order not to include extraneous matter. 

The dangers in shifting a base were well illustrated in a famous poll of public opinion conducted by a leading publication. In trying to get an expression of various groups on a topic of the day, the basis of classification was shifted several times. For example, questionnaires and ballots were first mailed to college graduates, then to home owners, and then to professional people. Some men received as many as three or four ballots, because they were not only college graduates, but home owners and professional men as well. The poll, which purported to be a cross section of American life, obviously fell short of its purpose because of duplication. People who knew of such instances were unduly skeptical of results. In keeping a subject file for mailing purposes, this danger must always be borne in mind, not only to prevent waste of postage but to avoid the scorn of the patron who receives five letters telling him "this offer is being made only to a selected few."

Subdivisions of a subject.-When a subject file becomes bulky, the main topics must be broken down. The subtopics are frequently arranged in alphabetical order. One of the common files in an office is that of "Insurance." It is quite impossible to refer to a policy or letter readily if all material is kept in one folder. New folders will

Filing probably be made to cover the general groupings of insurance used in the office, somewhat as follows: 

Insurance, Accident

Insurance, Automobile 

Insurance, Burglary

Insurance, Casualty 

Insurance, Fire 

Insurance, Group 

Insurance, Registered Mail

If policies make the folders too bulky to handle, a double division of the subject of insurance may be made so that the front section of folders may be used for correspondence and the back section for policies. Each section will include a folder for the various headings grouped under insurance. 

The subject index. Since you cannot govern the number of subjects treated in any single piece of material that is to be filed, it is usually necessary to set up a subject index. This consists of 3" X 5" cards, filed either alphabetically or by subject. 

The title of the subject treated will be typed on a card, below which will appear directions for locating the file, and often a digest of the contents. The cards may also be cross-indexed to show location of material which might be thought of as appearing under other headings. The following arrangement might be applied to the cards made out for a policy covering a group of officers in the organization: 

GROUP INSURANCE 

John Hancock Insurance Policy #1497235 9/14/29 

Covering class one officers.

JOHN HANCOCK INSURANCE COMPANY 

Policy #1497235 9/14/29

Group insurance covering 

Class one officers.

OFFICERS' INSURANCE John Hancock Insurance Policy 

#1497235 9/14/29 Group policy covering class one The three cards must be typed and put into the index box to make it easy to find material put in a bulky file.

Time element in operation of indexed files.— 

As a secretary, you will generally find your time at a premium. Consequently, your greatest problem in maintaining a subject file will be the ever-present danger that, in the rush of other work, the card index may be improperly made out or slighted. 

Only a full realization of the hopeless muddle that will result if the entries on the cards are deficient can save you from inefficiently operating an extensive subject file. For this reason, be sure, before installing such a system, that its merits far outweigh the difficulties you may encounter. 

A filing department which makes a business of keeping correspondence will be much better able to supervise a complicated filing system properly than will the busy secretary who has many other duties encroaching upon filing time.

Numerical filing.—When a number is assigned to each paper, there is little excuse for disorder in the files. Forms on which numbers are printed are

Filing 101 especially easy to arrange. When these numbers must be entered by hand, extra care should be taken to write the figures correctly and legibly. Do not make the mistake, for example, of copying 731 for 713.

Invoices, checks, orders, and similar instruments are commonly filed numerically. These documents are so important that the chance of error must be reduced to a minimum. When you refer to anything in a numerical file, check the numbers carefully. The slightest deviation in copying a number may necessitate hours of work in locating a paper. 

The only other key is usually the date, which may mean that a thousand orders will have to be gone over before the right paper on which the wrong number was reported is turned up. Accuracy is especially important in writing letters which refer to an invoice number of another firm. Lack of courtesy in checking your figures may cause much inconvenience to your correspondent. 

You may use a numerical arrangement to simplify a subject file. For example, to your employer may be committed the task of interviewing prospective employees. Suppose the only positions for which applications are received are for sales clerks, bookkeepers, and shipping clerks, and that in each case they are to be classified on the basis of experience or lack of experience. You might set up an index for the applications received as follows: 

1 Sales clerks a Experienced b Inexperienced

2 Bookkeepers a Experienced b Inexperienced 

3 Shipping clerks a Experienced b Inexperienced If the index number for applications were 600, the individual classification number would follow. 

Thus an application from an inexperienced bookkeeper would be filed 600-26. The number 600 indicates that the form is an application for a position; 26 indicates that the applicant is an inexperienced bookkeeper. 

The application would be placed in the folder containing all forms 600-2b, in its proper alphabetical order. Time sequence might be provided for by starting new files monthly, quarterly, semiannually, or yearly.

The Dewey system. The Dewey classification, prepared by Melvil Dewey and used extensively by libraries, divides the entire field of human knowledge into nine groups, with a tenth covering cyclopedias, periodicals, and works of too general a character to be placed in any of the nine divisions. 

This system uses a combination of subject and numerical index. 

The ten groups are: 

000 General works 

100 Philosophy 

200 Religion 

300 Sociology 

400 Philology 

500 Natural science 

600 Useful arts 

700 Fine arts 

800 Literature 

900 History

690 Building com- If Engineering, 620, (or any one of the other divisions) were taken, it, too, might be broken down into nine subdivisions:

The decimal system, as the Dewey system is sometimes called, is generally maintained by an extensive filing department, and the secretary is seldom called upon to install one. It is well, however, to be familiar with the general scheme as outlined above, in order to make intelligent use of a library.¹ 

¹ Books describing the Melvil Dewey system may be obtained at most public libraries. The Library of Congress has worked out a system of this kind for indexing the unlimited variety of books submitted for copyright. It is commonly called the "L. C. 

System." A descriptive pamphlet can be procured from the 

Superintendent of Documents, Washington, D. C., for a small fee.

Geographical filing.-When a firm's business is divided into territories, it is usually advisable to install some form of geographic filing in order that each division may be clearly identified. The basis may be branch office territories; sections covered by different salesmen and distributing agents; or political units such as states, counties, towns, or wards. Under these broad geographic headings the supplementary arrangement may be alphabetic, topical, chronological, numerical, or, as is frequently the case, a combination of all or several of these principles. 

Suppose you are keeping a customers' credit file from which you approve for shipment orders sent in by the salesmen. It is easier to have all names in the Philadelphia territory in one division, and those belonging to Detroit territory in another. 

The files will be less unwieldy, and by their setup will enable several people to work at them simultaneously.

Special types of files. The foregoing review of the principles upon which filing systems are built should aid you in applying the fundamentals of filing. Now it will be advisable to consider some of the commonly used special types of files which you, as a secretary, may wish to adapt to some particular work in your office. 

The tickler file.-Tickler files are the mainspring of efficiency in any office. They may take the form of a simple calendar index, a card file, or a chronological folder file. Any of these forms will serve

Filing 105 99 to bring matters to your mind. Memory is a wonderful thing, yet it cannot be trusted too far. 

A girl became secretary to a man who prided himself on his memory. Everything he told her caused her to make a shorthand note on her memorandum pad. The first few days he became much annoyed and asked her to "remember some things. 

She laughingly replied, "I shall when I know something to remember." During the next week she was frequently reminding him that he promised to get some data for another officer, that he had an engagement, or that he was expected to go to a meeting. Within a month he had learned to depend upon her shorthand notations to such an extent that, when he was not certain she had heard an appointment, he would ask, "Will you make a note of that for me, Miss Smith?" Your value will increase directly in proportion to your ability to keep a tickler file.

The calendar pad.-In many offices a calendar pad is all that is needed to keep full and accurate records of things which are to be done. Often these daily memorandum sheets are divided into hourly periods. 

As each item is completed, draw a line through the notation. In this way you can tell when you have taken care of all matters. Transfer a notation to the next day's work if advisable.

Recurrent items like lodge dues, rent, insurance premiums, taxes, and anniversaries should be placed on the calendar for the entire year. If you do not have time to finish the yearly schedule

at one time, make a note on the last entry to indicate that the notations have not been completed. 

In this way you will guard against not having a reminder on some date that the insurance premium is due.

The card index.-The card index tickler usually has a dated guide, consisting of thirty-one numbers, which divides a month's notations. As each day's work is finished, the guide for that date is placed at the back of the box to provide for that same date the following month. It is advisable to paste a small calendar sheet for both the current and the following month in the cover of the box so that a glance may confirm each date. This eliminates guessing about the dates upon which certain days of the week fall. At the beginning of each month, go through the file and remove the guides of all dates falling on Sundays and holidays. Placing these in the back of the file precludes the possibility of scheduling work for dates when the office is closed.

As you find that certain matters are to be taken up at some future date, make out a card similar to the following: 4/20/31 

Shall probably hear from James Smith today regarding acceptance of our offer. Write him if no word by 5/1/31.

A number of cards placed with the one bearing the above notation, under date of April 20, will serve

Filing 107 as reminders of different matters which must be given attention on that day. As each task is completed, destroy the card. If the card directing attention to James Smith's acceptance has not been removed at the end of the day, transfer it to the next day's business. Repeat this operation until May 1, when you will see that a letter is sent to Mr. Smith. 

Between April 20 and May 1, however, you have been constantly reminded to be on the alert for the receipt of the acceptance.

The chronological folder file.-The calendar pad and the card file are merely indexes which do not provide space for storing materials necessary for carrying out their daily instructions. For this reason some firms make extensive use of the dated folder file, sometimes called the "up file," which has an advantage in being large enough to include necessary papers.

As the name indicates, the file contains material which must come up to the executive on the day specified. For example, each bill, as it arrives, is put into the dated folder to insure payment in time to take cash discounts. Letters which need future attention are filed under the date when the matter is to come up again. The secretary removes the current folder from the cabinet upon arrival each morning, in order to go over the business for the day.

The folder system is very helpful where instructions are given to various persons in the concern by the executive. In such cases you make two

copies of the instructions, one to send to the subordinate who is to carry out the instructions, and the other to place in the "up file" until the day when the instructions are to be carried out. The executive is in position to make inquiries at that time as to whether the job has been completed. If inquiry indicates a delay, a notation is made of the cause of the delay and the time by which the work is promised. The instructions are then refiled, to be followed up again on a future date. 

Officials who pay the firm's bills find that the folder system enables them to write checks covering payments which fall due during a period they are to be away from the office. You should attach each check to the invoice and put the folder back in the safe. When the day arrives for payment, all you have to do is mail these checks. The folder tickler is especially valuable in real estate offices where rent, insurance, taxes, and other important items need prompt attention. 

Odd moments may be utilized by you in addressing envelopes for the checks, in writing letters of transmittal, and in otherwise anticipating work which may come on a busy day. 

The docket file.-A concentrated form of subject filing commonly used in certain types of business, but which is often not generally understood, is the docket file. Each letter or instrument, as it comes in, is placed in its subject folder in chronological order and bound. Papers arranged in the form of a tablet can be inspected without danger of loss

Filing 109 through any becoming loose. When the subject is completed, the docket is closed. Before the packet is placed in the "completed business" section of the file, an inscription, of which the illustration below is typical, is placed on its side. 

GREENWOOD ELEVATOR COMPANY, 

116 Bank Street, New York City 

Equipment installed in 

Curtis Building 

1817 East Street, Syracuse, N. Y. 

Contract awarded April 18, 1930 

Final inspection January 7, 1931 

File number C-1843

Docket filing is used extensively in law offices where it is desirable to have all papers on a given case neatly assembled. Contractors often use a double docket folder for keeping records of building operations—one side for legal papers such as the original contract and agreements for sub-letting parts of the contract, and the other side for correspondence, bills, and other papers. When the building is completed, the docket is closed and filed until the firm is no longer legally liable for any of the work. 

Investment banking houses use docket filing in their purchasing departments for recording matters relative to security issues which they sponsor, and

in their syndicate departments for keeping data on particular syndicate operations. 

The overlapping envelope file.-A visible index of the contents of envelopes may be made by using some form of the overlapping envelope file. Each envelope is placed in a frame which forces the top edge just a little above that of the envelope below it. This makes it possible to write the name or index on the visible space. Contents of such a file are usually alphabetically or numerically arranged. In typing the inscription at the top of the envelope, begin each name an equal number of spaces from the edge so the list will appear straight when envelopes are inserted under one another. 

A saw-toothed right-hand margin makes the finding of a certain envelope difficult. 

The holder is sometimes a steel frame with grooves in which the envelopes are inserted. The upright type of file is valuable in such places as payroll and registration offices, but is often unsightly in a private office where the flat or tablet holder can be used to better advantage. A similar file may be used for cards, hundreds of cards being attached to an upright file with several wings, or in a book file with a number of leaves. 

The clipping file. The clipping file is usually constructed on a subject basis, though sometimes classification is left entirely to a comprehensive index. Either a loose leaf or a bound book may be used, the size of which will depend upon the volume of clippings it is estimated will accumulate. In

Filing 111 some cases clippings are posted on loose sheets to be placed in a folder. In any event, do not paste. clippings as you would pictures in a kodak album, for this method takes up needless space. It is not necessary to see the entire article at a glance, as is the case when looking at a photograph. Paste only the top edge of the clipping so that the next one can be inserted underneath it. The top edge of the second clipping should be pasted directly below the place where the first one was fastened. 

This overlapping makes it possible to attach an incredible number of items on a single page. The disorder incident to any pasting process may be eliminated by using specially glued clipping book fillers. 

Clipping agencies will comb thoroughly through current literature for articles on any designated subject. These bureaus will be found listed in a classified telephone directory under "Newspaper 

Clippings." A very famous aviator is said to have asked a clipping agency to send his mother all articles mentioning a flight he was about to make. 

Later events made the flight such a news event that every paper in the country carried accounts of it. 

The mother was quickly compelled to do something to check the efforts of the clipping service, which had resulted in an avalanche of items being sent to her. 

While the clipping bureau service is valuable in making a thorough survey of current literature on any one subject, a variety of interests will necessitate finding your own material. You can do this best by going through the papers with a

colored pencil in hand to mark the articles you plan to save. Write the name of the publication and the date of issue across the top of each article. 

After the reading and labeling is finished, you can quickly cut out the marked items. This method enables you to choose between two articles appearing on opposite sides of a paper. If you clip the first article before you have read the second, you may miss the latter altogether, and it may be the more important of the two. If you want both items, get another copy of the paper. Back numbers of a paper or magazine may be procured for an extra charge by sending to the publishers or their dealers.

Indexing. The index to a file may either be in the form of guides on the files themselves or a separate listing on cards. It should contain all information necessary to locate given material. 

Place similar information in a uniform position in the index. Typewritten inscriptions are usually preferable, because handwriting lacks uniformity.

If you are indexing magazine articles, you will probably use the following arrangement: 

1. Your classification. 

2. The name of the article. 

3. The name of the author. 

4. The name of the publication. 

5. The date. 

6. A notation as to value, contents, etc. (This item may be omitted when its contents are connoted by the title of the article.)

Filing 113 7. Where the article is to be found. (If it is to be found under the classification indicated in item 1, number 7 is omitted.) 66 Cross-indexing is a part of the filing job that is usually neglected. If you are going to file a letter under "Instructions," it will probably be well to make out another card for the memorandum under 'Accounting Department" and still another under “James Grant," the accountant to whom the instructions are addressed. Of course, this involves the making of three cards, but it will help you find an elusive letter or memorandum when you have forgotten the heading under which it was filed. 

Codes are extensively used in indexes, especially in numerical and subject files. Beware of misinterpreting the code when you assign a symbol. 

Suggestions for keeping files in order. If filing is to be an important part of your work, you will probably wish to make a thorough study of the subject. The breadth of the field is indicated by the great number of books entirely devoted to its study and by the fact that one recent examination on filing was nine hours in length. 

Become familiar with some of the commercial indexes if you are keeping trade information. The people who compile these indexes spend a great · deal of time in determining the best titles for your particular trade. You can improve and simplify your work by comparing the subject titles you are using with those used in these printed indexes and adapting such good features as you may find.

Use a stapling machine to fasten papers together. 

Clips will make your files bulky and pins are apt to prick your fingers. The staple should be attached at the upper left-hand corner of the letter, the accepted place for fastening papers together. 

Subject classifications written for filing purposes should appear in the upper right-hand corner of the letter, so that they can be seen when glancing at the date. Some letterheads have a place provided for typing the subject and many firms insist that the subject be typed on the line below the salutation. Even though the title is not marked on the original letter, it should be put on the carbon copies. When the title on an incoming letter does not correspond with your file heading, be sure to write your own classification.

A colored pencil mark underscoring the filing index-whether the address, typewritten subject, firm name in the letterhead, or signature of the letter will help you when you are ready to file, if the subject is not specially written under the date. This underscoring at the time of original reading or filing will make it unnecessary to reread any letter which you may have occasion to refile. 

If you keep a card index to your subject file, always indicate when the subject was opened up. 

Then you will not have to go back over files made inactive before the new subject was added. 

Duplicating letters. Make several copies of a letter if you cannot determine offhand exactly under which heading it should be filed. It may

Filing 115 be that this particular letter should be cross-filed under several headings. In this way you will be able to locate one of the copies when it is requested. 

If you feel that making the extra copies entails too much work, you can save time by writing the address on a sheet and indicating the heading under which you have filed the letter. File this sheet in the folder for which you have no copy. 

Use of colored cards and clips.-Colors are used extensively to indicate which customers are prospects for special lines. Certainly it would be futile for an electric supply company to circularize a woman living in a hotel apartment with literature on washing machines. By putting prospects for radios on pink cards and prospects for washing machines on yellow ones, the sales department can sort cards quickly when a special sales effort on any one item is to be launched. 

Colored cards and clips are often used to call attention to special information. The color is in the nature of a code and has the advantage of being understood only by those using the data. A red card in a box of white filing cards will clearly indicate that a customer is a questionable credit risk without necessitating any derogatory comment in writing.

Removable signals may be used to indicate when a customer's account is past due. These signals may be paper pasters or the movable clips, which can readily be changed in position or replaced by a signal of another color.

The fact that many customers are circularized on several articles makes it necessary to duplicate a name on cards of several different colors. Highly efficient systems operated with perforated cards make selection almost automatic. A patented selector goes through and picks out all cards through which a hole has been punched in a position to indicate a prospect for a washing machine. Only one card is needed for a prospective customer of a number of products because perforations may be made in different positions on the card to indicate various products. This principle may be used in smaller systems, but hand selection, naturally, is slower. 

Handling odd-size reports. If odd-size reports are sent to you, it may be necessary to fold them to fit an ordinary filing cabinet or book binder. Do not go to the expense of having a special binder made for such reports, unless you are sure they will be continued over a long period of time. When such unstandardized reports arrive, call your employer's attention to the fact that they do not fit into standard filing equipment. Possibly they may be changed to standard size, or, if it becomes necessary to route them to a number of departments, modern methods of photostating, which permit the making of photostats of standard size regardless of the size of the original, may be used. 

Protecting the integrity of your files.-Protect yourself by making careful notations when someone takes a folder or a letter from your file. If you are careful in filing, there is no reason why you should

If you ask a man some such indefinite question as, "Did you take our purchase folder?", he will probably defensively answer "No." If, on the other hand, you tactfully ask, "Are you through with the purchase folder you borrowed from our files last 

Friday?", the individual will usually make every effort to think what he did with that folder. "Letter hunting is a costly sport. The responsibility for taking a letter from a file should be definite. "1

instruction to a file clerk to get a certain letter and send it to an individual who accepts responsibility for it. Later the clerk will not have to spend hours searching for that letter because her record will show who has it. As a secretary, you may keep a very small file and requests for your material may be too infrequent to warrant having a printed card system. It is advisable, however, to keep a few typed cards, which may easily be filled in, on hand in the front of your file. Without some guide, you will omit necessary information when you hurriedly make a memorandum that someone is taking part of your correspondence.

If you give a man a letter to which is clipped a notation to return the letter to you, he is not likely to forget where he got that paper. At the same time clip another card to your folder to indicate the disposition of its contents. Many secretaries prefer letter-size sheets for recording missing correspondence, because the card may slip down in the folder where it cannot easily be seen. 

A time allowance for borrowers is usually a very effective way to speed the return of papers. By asking the person when he will be able to return the file, you impress upon him his responsibility in caring for the material. If you appear with a written record that a certain file was to have been returned yesterday, the offender, realizing that you are supervising your files systematically, will probably try to return future material promptly.

Filing 119 The location of correspondence permanently removed from a folder should be carefully noted on the folder.

Physical care of contents of files. Close the drawers of your files when you are not using them. 

Picking up the scattered contents of a file drawer is usually the last straw needed to make a day a total loss. Even efficient secretaries sometimes have the very annoying habit of pushing drawers only part way shut. Aside from the danger of personal injury from walking into protruding corners, nothing makes an office look more untidy than several drawers that are partly open.

Lock the files when you leave for the day. After some material has been unceremoniously removed from them, you will probably learn this duty from bitter experience. One firm spent a large sum for a fireproof safe, but the secretary was prone to go home without locking it. Repeated warnings failed to impress her with the importance of this duty. 

One night the building burned and everything in the safe was destroyed. Because the office equipment company could not prove beyond a doubt that the safe was not defective, it furnished a new safe, but it could not replace the charred contents. 

Some customers paid the firm; others took advantage of the accident and did not. Despite her protestations that the safe was locked, the secretary's integrity was in doubt. When a new office was opened, the firm took no further risks and dis-

pensed with her services. Do you need such a costly lesson? .

Danger of too many headings.-Secretaries often attempt to revise a file about which they know nothing. This revision is a hazardous proceeding and will probably cost your firm money, if it does not cost you your position. Folders should never be started indiscriminately without due consideration for their usefulness. A maze of folders is no guarantee that anything can be found in the files; in fact, the experienced worker views them with distrust. One veteran secretary told the writer, "I have learned to pray before I make up a new subject heading. When I first started out, I made a folder for everything and I could find nothing. 

Certainly a period of meditation will help you to reduce the number of topics by working out various combinations. Very often several folders are opened up for the same firm. G. C. Smith, George 

C. Smith, and Smith & Company may all be the same. Be careful to avoid such duplications. 

Make a cross reference where a letter is written to an individual in a firm, but file under the firm name unless the correspondence is of such a nature that the individual, rather than the firm, is clearly the important factor.

Care of the filing equipment. Do not throw things into the file, and avoid overcrowding. 

Make frequent use of the expansion devices on your files. At the same time do not overtax the capacity of files. When a file can no longer be enlarged, When

Filing 121 remove some of the material. A file that is choked with papers is difficult to handle and its contents. are in danger of being torn. Watch to see that edges of papers are not preventing the locks of your files from catching. One secretary locked her files for several weeks but two drawers could be easily opened. The janitor, instead of reporting this, took occasion to go over confidential records. 

Use of suspense folder. All too often correspondence is stored in drawers, only to be forgotten. Your desk may not be in order, but it need not conceal matters requiring attention. 

Many a person has placed a letter in his desk because he had no regular place for pending matters, and then has forgotten about it completely until the matter was brought to his attention with a jolt. It is hard indeed to convince an angry employer that you did not wilfully conceal a paper, when it is eventually brought to light. The usual attitude toward this type of slip-up was rather harshly, but forcefully, impressed upon a young man with these words: "Hades is paved with good intentions; it's attention we want around here!"

A suspense folder placed in the front of your file makes an excellent place to store letters which you are temporarily unable to file. While the problems raised by the receipt of a letter are current, the letter will often be needed for reference. If a letter is not called for during the first week, the chances of its being needed are greatly diminished. You will always be much more inclined to leaf quickly

A through the contents of this accessible suspense folder than you will to draw suspicion to yourself by starting to rummage through your desk. suspense folder should never become a "catch-all" for matter which you do not know how to file. It should only be used until you have time to get around to the filing of the daily mail. Above all, it should not be used instead of a chronological pending or tickler file.

Employers themselves are prone to put letters in their desk and forget all about them. When needed, you may be put to much discomfort trying to unearth something you never had. Try to insist upon receiving all papers, but if this is impossible, maintain diligent watchfulness to detect the stowing away of papers you will be expected to have. 

Filing in a typical office.-Besides the centralized correspondence file maintained in most offices, you may have a private office file, various card indexes, book files, and other catalogued lists under your personal supervision. Even the least of these may be your undoing if you are not careful at all times.

Remember that, even as with Caesar, "The evil that men do lives after them; the good is oft interred with their bones." No matter how excellent a secretary you may be, your employer will be impatient and curt and entirely forget your manifold good qualities if you cannot produce a document when he wants it. Keep the files strictly up to date, for you never know the hour nor the minute when something will be needed.

CHAPTER V The Ordering and Care of Supplies 

When we serve we rule. 

When we give we have. When we surrender ourselves we are victors. We are most ourselves when we lose sight of ourselves.-J. H. OLDHAM. 

The secretary as a housekeeper. The secretary is the office housekeeper in the true sense of that word. Though most offices do not expect you to do heavy cleaning, they do demand that you maintain an orderly place in which to work. It is said that men are better housekeepers because they get the needed brushes and devices for doing work well. 

Most offices are not niggardly about buying required supplies, so suggest the little things which will aid in making the place more livable. A dusting mitt or a piece of clean cheesecloth is much more appropriate for emergency use before a caller than a piece of worn-out underwear brought from home, even though the latter may make a better dust cloth. 

Do not try to practice a false economy which is neither sensible nor desirable. 

The janitor and the office boy.-Girls should not be so helpless that they cannot open windows or do other work when necessary, but they should not hesitate to make adequate use of janitor and messen- 124

The Ordering and Care of Supplies 125 

ger boy service. Insist on good work, but do not forget to comment on work that is well done. 

People who do menial labor have much less inspiration than those who do brain work, so they enjoy your appreciation much more than a person of higher position might. 

Assisting office cleaners.-Do not use office help to get out of everything you hate to do, but coöperate with other employees in every way possible.

Many parts of the office cleaning cannot be done by the janitor, because of important materials which must be moved. Occasionally you will find it wise to put on cleaning clothes and join forces with Rastus in clearing up some particularly unsightly mess. 

One young woman who spent a Saturday afternoon in wrapping up a roomful of blueprints proved to be such an efficient worker that the janitor took special care of her quarters afterward. Instead of losing respect for her position because of the help she rendered, he always had a high regard for her ability after that day.

Ordering supplies.-The inefficient housekeeper rushes to the delicatessen upon the arrival of unexpected guests, but household efficiency demands that the good hostess have on her shelves a supply from which she can prepare a carefully-planned "quick menu." Likewise, business efficiency demands that you check over your supplies so that you may not be compelled to make purchases or send to the supply room at odd times in the day. 

Keep a requisition sheet where you can constantly

add items to it during the day. In a large office, hand your order to the supply clerk at night so supplies may be delivered early in the morning. 

You should make yourself responsible for ordering all supplies, whether work of this sort must be done on your own initiative or through your employer. 

If you are making purchases covering any length of time, it is always well to make a memorandum of what you have ordered. These data put on your employer's desk will keep him informed of what is being done. However, there are two sides to this procedure which must be considered. Your employer may not want to be bothered with details and, if you ask his permission to order things which you should be perfectly able to procure by yourself, the undue talking about the matter may be annoying. The memorandum usually enables him to cancel orders of which he does not approve. Even seemingly safe purchases are sometimes unfortunate.

One secretary handed her employer a two years' supply of engraved name cards just an hour before it was publicly announced that his title had been changed by the directors of the organization. The promotion was no surprise to the man himself, but the outburst of disgust which he emitted upon receiving the cards was at least one reason which the secretary might have found for regretting his advancement. Mergers, consolidations, bankruptcy, and change of the firm name often cause perfectly well-intentioned ordering to become undesirable.

The Ordering and Care of Supplies 127 

Until you are perfectly sure of the absolute bounds of your authority, it is often well to err on the side of caution. One should make every effort to have duties clearly defined. However, it is well to remember that some men are not capable of totally releasing their hold on even minor details. When they are busy, a secretary may do much to relieve them and will be censured if she does not do so, but when they have an idle minute to themselves these men are prone to revert to their former habit of assuming duties that they have not been performing for some time. Unexpected acts of this type are frequently most exasperating to an efficient secretary. For example, one girl had been ordering supplies in her office without instruction for years. 

No thought of overstepping her authority entered her mind when, after the yearly budget was made up, she placed an order for the year's supply of fifty thousand envelopes. Much to her discomfiture another fifty thousand envelopes arrived just a few days before her order was due. The employer, having been experiencing a lull in business, had gone out and ordered the supplies himself. The secretary's terror of consequences caused her to consult a secretarial group that evening in the hope of finding a way out of her dilemma. Of course, no set procedure which would work in every case could be prescribed. The fiery little secretary who advised that girl to "go in and jump him before he gets a chance to jump you" probably did know the right course of action; whether one would be wise to

carry it out in most cases is debatable. Forest and prairie fires are often controlled by building up a backfire of sufficient proportions to stop the progress of the blaze, but the fire of men's tempers is not always counteracted by the same means, especially if the man knows he has been in error and does not want to admit it. You must decide whether rightness will seem so important to you in case you are compelled to seek another position. 

Verifying receipts of materials. A great number of secretaries are extremely careless in checking up the receipt of supplies. Check materials against the requisition or the bill as you unpack them. 

Listings of omitted items should be clearly deleted from a bill and notations of items which are defective, broken, or of inferior quality should be perfectly clear. There should be at least one checking on every bill-the receipt of goods as listed. If prices are given, these should be checked with the original quotations. Extensions and additions should be verified. Sign your name to the checking you have done. Systematic attention to this duty will save your firm much money in the course of a year.

Usually reliable firms will make good on any articles found to be broken or defective. However, if credit is to be given, the wholesale house usually demands that the article be returned or shown to the salesman, even though it is too damaged or defective for future use. You will enable the seller to recover loss from the manufacturer or trace down

The Ordering and Care of Supplies 129 

insecure packing if you carefully preserve such goods. For this reason, when notifying a company of defective goods, always refer to the number or name on the packing slip if one can be found in or on the package.

Verify the contents before signing a receipt if verification is at all practicable. However, it is not always advisable or possible to keep a delivery man waiting until you have taken all supplies from the box and examined them. Nevertheless, watch to see that you are not signing a bill which says, "Goods received and found to be satisfactory," unless you have thoroughly examined them. Some secretaries write on bills, "Received but not examined." A rubber stamp may be used for putting this inscription above your name.

Quantity ordering. Use good judgment in the quantity of supplies you order. Paper usually shows a slight yellowing with age. A large supply of letterheads or printed office forms in your cabinet will prove very wasteful if another form is adopted. 

One secretary got a bargain on typewriter ribbons, so he bought a supply which he thought would last the office for five years. Before long the ribbons had dried out and become so rotten they would not endure more than two days' hard usage. 

Purchasing responsibility.-In buying for the office or for your employer, use judgment in selecting things that will serve the purpose well. Do not be afraid to spend money if you think your employer would want good things, yet do not use your

unlimited buying privilege to throw economy to the winds. Learn to buy goods because they suit the needs of your office-not because you like the salesman of a particular company. Personal preference, though always present, is easily seen if the quality and prices given by a house do not measure up to the standards set by competing firms. Tips, concessions, and favors which influence your choice are not worth the price you will pay in loss of confidence.

You will probably be called upon to purchase personal or family articles for a busy employer. 

The man who does not have a home, or the man whose wife's shopping time is limited by illness or by family cares, often finds a secretary's help invaluable. Develop judgment and ability as the office and personal purchasing agent of your employer. 

System and forethought in buying.-Though spontaneous buying of gifts is very fine in principle, the wise business man has these matters arranged according to some system whereby he cannot neglect them. Keep a calendar of the birthdays, anniversaries, holidays, and special events which your employer wishes to remember, so you can remind him of their approach. He may become so involved that he will neglect to buy a gift for mother's day, mail a remembrance on father's day, or get the all-important present on his own wedding anniversary. To the one slighted it will seem a thoughtless thing for him to have forgotten such an important event, but you who live through a busy office day

The Ordering and Care of Supplies 131 

will know how impossible it often is to remember anything which is not forced upon the attention. 

Even though the employer's memory has proved perfectly good, he may often be prevented from getting away in time to make the purchase. Help him to remember early enough either to get the gift himself or allow you to make the purchase for him. 

In mailing or sending gifts always see that the tags are removed.

Keep a supply of conservative cards of sympathy, condolence, and congratulations on hand. The business man who sends these cards to business acquaintances or associates who are experiencing some of life's joys or sorrows shows a thoughtfulness which marks him among men. Little remembrances are very much appreciated, even though the event may not call for a personal letter from a busy executive. You can often apprise your employer of a death or promotion notice which appears in the papers. Office employees generally feel more disposed to confide in you than in your employer. An executive who sends a card to an office boy who is graduating from night school, or a clerk who has lost his mother, does not succeed only in surprising the employee; he usually wins his undying devotion. 

Care of supplies. Most secretaries make the mistake of putting too many supplies in a desk.

To unload an entire box of envelopes or a package of letterheads in a desk drawer is destructive to both supplies and desk. The edges of the paper become torn or wrinkled and the drawer is strained because

it is too full to be worked smoothly. A reserve cabinet or drawer is always a good outlet, but if you have no storage space, try to avoid crowding by getting another secretary to take part of the contents of the box. Do not let your employer's supply of name cards and personal stationery become completely exhausted before ordering a new supply, because engraving sometimes requires time. 

Arrange correspondence materials in the desk so that copies are readily accessible in the order in which they are generally used. Try to keep everything in its place. Be especially careful to keep carbon paper in a folder where it will not become creased or rub off on other materials. 

Hunting may not always be an evidence that your desk is not in order, but it does reveal the fact that you have not thoroughly learned the order. If you give a little thought to working out a satisfactory arrangement of your desk, you will not be so likely to forget the place to put your materials.

Arrangement of office. The position of each piece of furniture should be carefully studied so that arrangement may be made whereby little walking will be necessary. Files should be near the secretarial desk rather than near that of the employer. Chairs should be placed in a position where they are not in the way of persons walking about the room. One chair should be placed so that a visitor can comfortably talk with your employer. Some offices find it necessary to place the employer's desk in such a position that the

The Ordering and Care of Supplies 133 

guest chair cannot be pulled up behind it. The "confidential" caller is so annoying that it may be well to arrange the office furniture so as to protect your employer from those who become so interested that they do not realize their physical proximity is obnoxious.

Reasons for changes. In rearranging an office it is well to remember "men like things that stay put; they are averse to change, becoming much disturbed when they come home to find the bed in a different corner of the room." The secretary has to introduce changes into the office sparingly and usually after consultation. A man is often sensitive to any intimation that feminine fickleness led to changes in office arrangement. He will feel much more secure in his position as commander of the office if he can readily answer any comment on a change with "Yes, the light was not good on Miss

Smith's desk," or "We found we needed more room for that new cabinet." For this reason, if you want to move anything, think out a sensible reason which your employer can use when called upon to make an explanation. The questionnaire which proved navy blue to be man's favorite color was hinted to have revealed only the fact that this was the only color name of which most men were perfectly sure. masculine love of certainty may be open to ridicule outside of the office, but it is an important consideration in arranging office equipment. This

Location of clocks.-Pulling out one's watch to look at the time before a caller is discourteous even

though business is run on a time schedule. You can save your employer by having the clock placed so that it is plainly visible to both visitor and employer. Winding the office clock was the duty by which the old-time employer judged his secretary's ability to carry out details. With the installation of electric clocks of all sizes, a new measuring rod will have to be sought. 

The secretary's desk. Your desk should not be placed against the wall because you must be aware of the entrance and exit of people into and from the office. Aside from this, turning your back on people creates an open temptation for someone to glance over your shoulder at the work in your machine. 

You should face your employer so that a mere glance from him may bring you to his aid.

Need for proper lighting. Go through any large office and you will find window space occupied by people who seldom sit at their desks, while the darkest spots in the room are assigned to secretaries. 

The fact that knowledge of lighting defects does not carry over into office consciousness was evidenced by one business man who, as a school director, spent much time and effort in insisting on the proper lighting of a new school building. He was very justly proud of his work, yet he did not realize that fifty girls in his stenographic department came out of that well-lighted school to seek close employment for twice as many hours a day in a room in which there was not even an adequate number of the oldfashioned glaring ceiling lights.

The Ordering and Care of Supplies 135 

Do your best to overcome the tendency to place the secretary's desk in a dark part of the room. 

Because your eyes are to be subjected to strain most of the day, try to secure proper artificial lighting of your desk if you find it impossible to get suitable daylight. The new fixtures which are displacing the long-distance glare of a few years ago are a blessing which you should seek for yourself. 

Preparation of the office for comfortable use. Be sure that office pens are filled and in place. See that fountain pens are frequently washed out in lukewarm water. Buy fountain pen fluid so as not to ruin gold points with poor ink. Place an unabridged dictionary in a convenient location, so that employers and employees can readily refer to this indispensable part of the equipment of any office. Also place a waste basket near each desk in the room. Every telephone should be provided with a pad and pencil for taking notes. Hush-aphones may prove a good investment if some of the voices have annoying carrying qualities. Telephone books with heavy, dark covers may be purchased and placed on desks where they can be easily reached. 

Few secretaries have learned the value of keeping a small supply of all materials on an emergency shelf. If a dozen envelopes, twenty-five letterheads, a few name cards, and a small number of all other forms were constantly kept in reserve, many an awkward situation could be averted. Replace supplies promptly when emergency has caused you to draw upon this reserve.

Office flower service. The flower service inaugurated by florists in some cities probably gives more joy to the office and its callers than any like amount of money spent in beautifying the office. A flat rate of one hundred fifty dollars a year will deliver a bouquet to the office each Monday, Wednesday, and

Friday of the year. Because each day brings a different type of flower, it is necessary to have about three containers. The large green glass bowl with a wire screen can be adapted to most bouquets, but it is well to provide a deep spindle vase for the longer stems and a medium-sized vase for the days when only a very few of the more expensive flowers are sent. The opening and care of these prize packages usually falls to the lot of the secretary, so go to a florist to learn how to arrange flowers. A great deal of beauty can be brought out through artistic arrangement. Aspirin put in the water will preserve the flowers well for the two days. 

Caring for the employer's desk. The care of the employer's desk is sometimes assumed by the secretary. This duty is performed during the employer's absence unless he prefers to have you work with him. Keep the desk supplied with clean folders for concealing matter not in use. Never put letters on the desk with the face up; turn the first one over or inclose all in a folder. The leather-bound tablet folder is very satisfactory, the different compartments forming storage space for different materials without danger of mixing the papers.

The Ordering and Care of Supplies 137 

Be alert to remove papers and materials as their use is completed. A wooden desk tray, similar in finish to the desk, is an excellent place for the employer to put things which he wishes you to take away. Besides a wooden tray and a leather folder, the desk should have a desk blotter, a calendar, a fountain pen holder with pen, and a holder filled with memorandum slips. Every effort should be made to keep things down nearly to this minimum, in order that the desk may be easily taken care of.

Respecting private property.-Some employers detest having a secretary interfere with anything on their desks. There is no reason why they should have a secretary trespassing just because she has been taught to keep a desk in order. Allow your employer to keep his desk any way he wants it, without giving him a guilty feeling that he is eccentric in having this preference. There is certainly a happy medium between the officer who has nothing on his desk and the individual who does not even give his domain the traditional spring and fall cleaning. However, remember that the desk belongs to your employer, so you are only called upon to give him the help he desires. With the smaller living quarters in vogue today, many business men find their office desks the only place on earth which they can call their very own. Always see that your employer has at least one drawer in his desk in which both you and he understand it will be possible for him to keep anything in complete

privacy without the necessity of a key to insure its seclusion. 

Tolerance of careless tendencies. You may not approve of the order of your employer's desk, but do not create an antagonistic attitude toward your help by insinuating that he is not neat. It is well to remember that it is a human failing to be unnecessarily neat about one thing and careless about another. Your employer may be a really great man, even though a disorderly desk now hides that fact from you. Consider the lifelong friendship between two boys which was terminated completely in a college dormitory because one never polished the brass faucets on the bathtub and the other left his bureau drawers open about an inch. 

While everyone else regarded both boys as scrupulously neat, their mutual recriminations led to open battle. Tolerate others' weaknesses, for you have a great many of your own. 

Cleaning files. You can seldom give your files a complete, old-fashioned housecleaning, but you should keep constantly at the work of putting them. in order. Start at the beginning in some of your spare moments, rearranging a folder at a time. 

Put a marker in a conspicuous position so that you can quickly resume the work. It will be surprising how easily you can complete the task without the disorder which usually accompanies cleaning efforts. 

Physical care of files. Provide reinforcements for the punched holes in book fillers. Go over book files periodically to reinforce leaves that have been

The Ordering and Care of Supplies 139 

torn out. Reinforce or provide new folders for those which become damaged through constant or careless use.

Uneven growth of correspondence causes some folders to fill up much more quickly than others. 

A crowded folder should not always be transferred to an inactive file, even though some subdivision of its contents is necessary. Keep the older material active by placing it in a second folder behind the current folder. Mark both opening and closing dates plainly on the folder of older material and the date of beginning on the newer material. 

Disposition of inactive matter. The disposition of material into inactive files always raises two questions which you should study carefully: 

1. When shall I consider material inactive? 

2. What shall I throw away?

Little deviation from a strict periodic transfer of regular files is usually considered most effective. 

However, continuous transfer systems, based upon a specified limit of time for names to be kept in a file, are easily operated. Continuous transfer is especially effective in the keeping of a mailing list file, the names being discarded when no business has been done with a firm over a period of time. If all mailing lists were subjected to such a systematic transfer rule, letters would not be sent to people many years after their death. Discarded lists form an excellent basis for a follow-up campaign by a department which may be interested in ascertaining

reasons for discontinuance of trade relations with the house.

Conservation of valuable records.-Space is valuable in most offices, so it is impossible to keep all records indefinitely. However, do not go blithely about tearing up everything in the files, as is often done at the end of a six-month period. Never ship away, burn, or otherwise indiscriminately dispose of even inactive files. Usually it is advisable to keep the files of a completed period in an inactive file for a certain time. This practice will bring to light a number of things that will be revived. 

You will need much experience in the business to know what to discard. Use spare moments in this selection process. After much material has been destroyed, carefully pack and label the more important matter, so future reference may be made to it if necessary. This system will save searchers much time and annoyance at a time when nerves are usually on edge. You cannot always keep your files in order if a number of people have access to them, but have them in order, chronologically and alphabetically, before packing them away. In most states suits for collections cannot be brought after seven years. Litigation files should be carried for this length of time at least.

The waiting room.—If you have a private waiting room for your employer's guests, put thought into its arrangement. Try to improve on the illarranged places where people are usually compelled to sit and watch the office traffic go past while any-

The Ordering and Care of Supplies 141 

one is privileged to stare at them. The private waiting room has many advantages, as does the private conference room, but its arrangement must take into consideration the fact that the guests entertain themselves in this place. Be sure that the room is clean and well aired. Give special attention to the temperature both in summer and winter. If you go into the room occasionally during the day, you will be able to report temperature or disorder to the people who can adjust them. The room should be supplied with cold drinking water, and individual drinking cups if a thermos pitcher is used. One thoughtfully planned waiting room has framed instructions on where to locate toilet and smoking rooms.

Comfortable chairs and a table or desks should form part of the equipment of every waiting room. 

Secretarial literature has said so much about the necessity of providing magazines for visitors that many secretaries indiscriminately thrust a paper into a visitor's hands as soon as he is seated. This has become most annoying to many people, because the ordinary short wait can be used in thinking out private problems or in getting acclimated to the office. Reading material should be placed in racks where the caller may voluntarily choose what he wants. In ordering periodicals for a visitor's comfort, it is well to remember that his reading time is limited. Choose books that are meant to be dipped into from time to time instead of being read through from cover to cover. Nothing is more disturbing

than to become engaged in reading something interesting and then be called away without being able to finish. Your company's own literature, trade periodicals, good newspapers, travel magazines, books with pictures, poetry, and current magazines will provide appropriate reading matter. 

Ability to advise and suggest. Most employers welcome suggestions in buying equipment or making a change of system. Sometimes letterheads which are carried over long periods of time are chosen with little thought. If you show an interest in office stationery, changes may be made which will place the office on a higher plane. Paper of a white or neutral shade is chosen by houses of highest standards. Letterheads with gaudy pictures on them may be replaced by ones which have only a neat trademark with the name and address of the concern. Envelopes should be opaque so that contents cannot be read. Two sizes are usually sufficient for correspondence. 

Acquaintance with standard supplies.—You can be of great help in ordering supplies if you know something about standard materials. If you ask for a book binder 17½" × 2934", it will often be made up for you without question. You are expected to exercise judgment, and the buyer shows his confidence in your ability by not questioning your requisition. Do you know enough about supplies to justify such confidence? Talk to salesmen, go to business shows, and look through office

The Ordering and Care of Supplies 143 

equipment catalogues to inform yourself on this part of your work.

Standardization of filing equipment makes it advisable, from the standpoint of economy, to confine all forms as nearly as possible to the letter size (81½" x 11") and the library card size (3″ x 5″).

Other standard sizes, taken from a table prepared by the Hammermill Paper Company, which may be cut without waste are indicated on page 144. 

Special sizes are expensive and usually soon outlive their usefulness.

Study of individual office needs.-Accustom yourself to the materials used in your particular office in order to superintend their ordering and care. However, do not allow yourself to continue things over a long period of time because they have been traditionally used there. Your business is a growing and expanding organization, so your equipment must be molded to fit its changing needs. Be alert to detect improvements which may be made. The inventor is the one who sees possibilities that are not observed by those who are completely absorbed in the everyday operation of a machine. 

Do not be afraid to make suggestions tactfully for the betterment of your office. A machine sorts with automatic precision, but the wide-awake secretary, by getting a mental vision of the needs of an organization, adds to this machinelike precision the results of thinking.
